::: {.hero}
## Heterogeneity of treatment effect analysis for randomized trials

Which patients benefit, by how much, and how confident can we be? An end-to-end
pipeline combining Bayesian machine learning with randomization-based inference —
published with its code, so it can be applied to your own trial.
:::

## The problem

A trial reports one average treatment effect. Clinicians want to know something
different: *does this therapy work for the patient in front of me?*

Standard subgroup analysis answers a related but weaker question — which
covariate-defined groups have different **average** effects — and does so one
binary split at a time, with limited power and a multiplicity problem.

This pipeline attacks the question from two directions at once, and keeps them
clearly separated.

## Two complementary approaches

::: {.card-grid}

::: {.analysis-card}
### Model-based

**Parts I–III.** Bayesian Additive Regression Trees estimate a conditional
average treatment effect for every patient. A regression tree is then fitted *to*
those estimates, turning a per-patient vector into interpretable, covariate-defined
subgroups. Sensitivity analyses check the result against the BART priors and
against other estimators.

Answers: *which measured covariates drive the effect?*
:::

::: {.analysis-card}
### Randomization-based

**Part IV.** Confidence bounds on the quantiles of the individual treatment
effects, using no outcome model at all — only the trial's own randomization.
Finite-sample exact, at the cost of returning bounds rather than point estimates.

Answers: *what fraction of patients actually benefit?*
:::

:::

The distinction matters. A flat CATE surface in Parts I–III is **not** evidence
that individual effects are constant — those methods are conditional-mean
analyses and are structurally incapable of detecting heterogeneity driven by
unmeasured factors. Part IV is the analysis that speaks to it.
